title: Network & Transport: The Executive Decisions
say: Welcome. This is the executive briefing for Book 09 of the Federal Modernization Workbook, Network and Transport. It's for the people who fund, authorize and answer for the branch network: the CIO, the CISO, network program executives and budget owners. It's built around decisions, not configuration. For each one, I'll say what has to be decided, who owns it, and when it's needed. Four questions organize the half hour. Why act now, when the target architecture is years away. What federal policy actually requires, and where the money should go first. Who decides each step. And how to proceed without turning a faster network into a weaker one. Here's the short version. No product shortens a fiber path. So buy transport on physics, govern it as compliance, and decide in the right order. Let's start with the decisions this briefing asks for.

title: Seven decisions this briefing asks for
say: This briefing asks for seven decisions, each with a named owner. None is a product choice, and none needs an award to start. Several cost nothing but a signature and a few weeks of staff time. The expensive mistakes come from leaving them unmade while circuits, refreshes and migrations move ahead on their own schedules. In short: the CISO ends managed TIC circuits only when CISA confirms the replacement telemetry. The authorizing official records today's gap as an accepted risk, before an assessor finds it. Security architecture writes the target into the edge-device refresh that BOD 26-02 is forcing anyway. The sponsor and CIO put staff time and requirements work before capital, test the field-office refresh request against published capacity limits, and tie the retirement of the Windows RADIUS server to the Entra migration, not to a date. And the authorizing official and system owner hold the line on order: the governor is live before traffic moves. The thread through all seven is simple. Policy names no product, but it isn't requirement-free, and order and ownership decide the outcome. First, why act at all.

title: Transport is physics; control is compliance
say: Programs keep merging two different decisions, and that's where the risk starts. Choosing a pipe is a physics decision. Light in fiber covers about a kilometer every five microseconds. The voice budget leaves the network roughly 70 to 100 milliseconds, and on the book's worked arithmetic, a Seattle office hairpinning through northern Virginia spends about 60 milliseconds one way on geography alone. No product moves that floor. Local breakout fixes the geographic part, and nothing else. Choosing what governs the pipe is a compliance decision. Direct internet access solves the hairpin, but it satisfies none of the protection controls. Boundary protection, inspection and monitoring all come from the control layer. So here's what an executive should watch for. A branch moved from a governed hairpin to bare local breakout has lost assessed boundary protection. The book calls that a compliance regression with better latency. It looks like modernization on a dashboard, and it reads as a finding in an assessment. Every decision here keeps those two choices separate: buy the pipe on measured physics, and take the protection from the governor above it. Next, the clocks already running.

title: The external clocks are already running
say: The second reason to act is that the external clocks are already running, whether or not a network program is funded. FIPS 140-2 certificates moved to NIST's historical list on September 22, so new purchases should state the 140-3 expectation. The post-quantum memo, M-26-15, wanted agency migration plans by October 22, 2026. The first agency logging plan under M-26-14 is due November 18. BOD 26-04's third phase lands December 7, FedRAMP's 2026 rules become mandatory on January 1, and the EIS first option period ends July 31, 2027. The one that spends money is BOD 26-02. It requires identified end-of-support edge devices off agency networks by August 5, 2027. I'll come back to it, because it's the fork in the road for the whole branch architecture. Here's the honest part. Three of these requirements fall inside roughly fifteen months, and they all draw on the same network and security staff a branch-edge program would need. An agency promising an SD-WAN program next year alongside them is promising the same people twice. Say that plainly in the plan. And one clock has already run out: the legacy telecom contracts ended by May 31, 2026. Next, what happens if you don't act.

title: The risk of not acting is not standing still
say: Not acting doesn't mean standing still. Three things happen by default. First, money gets spent without a choice being made. The BOD 26-02 refresh will happen on a directive clock. Run as like-for-like replacement, it spends the money and closes the architecture question for the life of the new equipment. Deferral has a measured price too. GAO reported that billing for six agencies' legacy Networx contracts rose from about 13.4 million dollars in February 2025 to about 40.9 million in March, a 206 percent increase. Second, gaps surface as findings rather than accepted risks. The technical situation is identical; the institutional position isn't. And cutting managed TIC circuits before CISA confirms replacement telemetry trades a transport gap for a visibility gap, which is worse. Third, cost gets blamed on the cloud. When workloads migrate before transport is measured, slowness gets blamed on the only thing being measured, and cloud spend rises. The book labels that its own inference, a hypothesis to test in your estate. And under all three, the governor is attack surface. In February 2026, Emergency Directive 26-03 ordered action on Cisco SD-WAN systems after attackers compromised them. Whatever you buy, protect it before it carries traffic. Next, what TIC 3.0 actually requires.

title: TIC 3.0 as republished in September 2026
say: What does TIC 3.0 actually require? The book reads it from the current documents, not from what's said about them. CISA republished the whole set in September 2026, but the only changes were updated footnote links, so the substance dates from July 2025. There are four use cases: Traditional, Branch Office, Remote User and Cloud. There's no SASE use case. An agency deploying SASE at its branches operates under the Branch Office and Cloud use cases. TIC 3.0 sets goals, not methods. But two statements constrain a branch. Policy enforcement parity: once you decide a capability is needed, you apply it on every path, SD-WAN paths included. And preserve CISA's visibility as branches connect directly to outside services. CISA's June 2026 SASE guide adds that traffic doesn't have to route through TIC access points if an alternative gives both the agency and CISA situational awareness. That guide permits SASE. It doesn't require it. So when someone says TIC requires SD-WAN, or that TIC forbids local breakout, both claims fail. The honest position is narrower and stronger: local breakout is allowed, and the agency must show parity and preserve CISA's view on every path it opens. Next, the opposite mistake.

title: Technology-neutral is not requirement-free
say: The opposite mistake is just as common: concluding that because policy is technology-neutral, the branch is unconstrained. It isn't. Four binding obligations land on branch equipment, and none of them picks a product. Egress DNS must go to CISA's Protective DNS. Internet-exposed management interfaces come off the internet under BOD 23-02. End-of-support edge devices go under BOD 26-02. And anything terminating TLS or IPsec needs post-quantum key exchange under M-26-15. The obligations that bite hardest are often ones the agency wrote itself. Once a branch breaks out locally, it's an external boundary, and the security plan makes promises about it. That gap surfaces at assessment time, not deployment time. For budget owners, the other side matters too. No federal instrument requires SD-WAN or SASE, and none requires the WAN itself to be encrypted where the payload is already protected end to end. So an overlay is a risk decision, not a compliance obligation. And FedRAMP certifies cloud services, not the routes an agency uses to reach them. When a network change is refused on FedRAMP grounds, ask which control it violates. A refusal with no control basis is a governance failure, and should be recorded as one. Next, logging and telemetry.

title: Logging and CISA telemetry after MTIPS
say: Logging and CISA telemetry are where branch modernization most often goes wrong quietly. M-26-14 rescinded M-21-31 on May 22, 2026. Logs must be searchable for six months and retrievable for a year, and agencies must be able to show addresses, ports and session details. A branch with nothing at its edge doesn't produce that record. When branches leave the managed TIC service, the telemetry CISA has been receiving stops. The replacement is CLAW, CISA's log aggregation warehouse, and onboarding takes the agency, CISA and the provider working together. That's a three-party dependency with its own lead time, so it belongs on the critical path, starting in Phase 0. Here's the decision. The exit criterion for leaving MTIPS, and for ending each branch's MPLS, is confirmed CLAW parity, not branch cutover. Cutting circuits first trades a transport gap for a visibility gap. Ownership splits three ways on purpose. The CISO decides when parity is reached. Security operations confirms it, branch by branch. And only a contracting officer can terminate a contract, so the contracting officer ends the circuit, only after that confirmation. No engineer can cancel a circuit, however redundant it looks. Next, the long interim.

title: The long interim: the case by elimination
say: For many agencies, neither SD-WAN nor a new TIC use case is close. The acquisition isn't funded and the task orders aren't placed. The book calls that interval the long interim, and argues the architecture by elimination, because no mandate exists. The hairpin is still permitted, but CISA's own guidebook says it raised the cost and cut the effectiveness of TIC for cloud services. A new agency-run access point is a capital and staffing commitment. VPN backhaul is a hairpin under another name. What's left is local breakout, a cloud-delivered security stack nearby, and a policy layer at the branch edge. The target is years away for structural reasons: acquisition takes quarters, budget submissions go to OMB in September, and a thousand branches is a multi-year deployment on logistics alone. But the interval isn't empty. Four of the six branch-edge functions are partly obtainable before any award. The decision belongs to the authorizing official. Record which control assertions depend on transport evidence that doesn't exist, the compensating measures, and the funded plan to fix them. An undocumented gap found by an assessor is a finding. A documented gap with a plan is an accepted risk. Do it now. Next, the most important planning item.

title: BOD 26-02 makes the refresh the fork in the road
say: This is the most important planning item in the book. BOD 26-02, issued February 5, 2026, puts branch edge hardware on a directive clock. Devices whose support ends by February 2027 come out then, and all identified end-of-support edge devices must be off agency networks by August 5, 2027. It covers internet-reachable boundary devices, so a branch router with its own internet circuit qualifies. An interior access switch may not, so don't assume the directive funds the access layer. For an agency with aging branch equipment, part of the capital it assumed it didn't have is going to be spent anyway, inside the window everyone calls years away. And a refresh is exactly when a branch architecture gets chosen again. The default is like-for-like, which spends the money and closes the question for the life of the equipment. The recommendation is narrow and cheap. Tell whoever is scoping the replacements, in writing, what the eventual target needs from a branch device, from application-aware steering and telemetry to post-quantum key exchange and a FIPS 140-3 expectation. Security architecture owns that decision, before the replacements are scoped, and acquisition writes it into every order. It costs requirements-writing time. Not doing it spends the same money and closes the option. Next, where to invest.

title: Where to invest, and in what order
say: Where should the money go, and in what order? The book lines its chapters up into five tiers, cheapest and most certain first. First, staff time, with no award: write the application-to-path policy the controls already ask for, instrument a sample of branches, and test, not just read, that DNS reaches CISA's Protective DNS. Second, requirements time: put the target into the BOD 26-02 refresh. Third, accreditation and CLAW onboarding. Circuits arrive in about a quarter; an authorized breakout architecture takes far longer. Fourth, protect the governor, with phishing-resistant MFA, hardening, fast patching and logs held off the box. Fifth, and only then, capital. One point on pricing. Moving from MPLS to internet access plus a cloud security service changes the cost driver from site count to user count, and the per-user security subscription is the line most likely to dominate, and the one most often left out. Price your own circuits in GSA's EIS pricer rather than citing a marketing number. And don't justify the program on latency alone; the stronger argument is governance and evidence. The sponsor and CIO set this order, and it needs to be settled before the next September budget submission. Next, a worked field-office case.

title: Field offices: fix the circuit, not the content
say: Field offices are where these decisions become a budget line. The book works a case many civilian agencies will recognize: about 1,500 field offices, about 70,000 endpoints, and a request for about 50 million dollars to refresh a Configuration Manager distribution point in every office. Three findings. First, the unit cost doesn't reconcile. That's 33,333 dollars per office, about twice the book's fully loaded server case, so the request needs to say whether it's acquisition or five-year cost. Second, capacity. Microsoft's published limit is 4,000 clients per distribution point, so the estate needs 24, two at each of 12 hubs. The other 1,476 exist only to make up for slow branch circuits. Third, timing. Microsoft says new device-management innovation happens in Intune, so hardware bought now depreciates past its likely use. The alternative fixes the circuit instead. On the book's planning assumptions, it needs about 10 million dollars of first-year capital and turns cumulatively positive in year four. But it hinges on one number: breakeven is 873 dollars of current MPLS cost per office per month. Below that, argue capability rather than savings. So the sponsor and CIO decompose the request and validate that MPLS figure before the refresh money is committed. Next, network access control.

title: Network access control: the last Active Directory tie
say: Network access control looks like an engineering topic. It reaches the executive agenda because it's usually the last piece of the network still standing on Active Directory. Windows Network Policy Server, the RADIUS server built into Windows, authorizes devices against Active Directory computer objects, and Entra joined devices don't support that. There's no Entra RADIUS service. So as the Entra migration progresses, NPS becomes less useful. And if it goes away before its replacement is validated, the result isn't a degraded experience. It's a total loss of network access. The older password methods are breaking on their own schedule, too. Credential Guard and the October 2026 Windows update are closing them off, so agencies on older guidance now have a deadline they didn't choose. The target is certificate-based authentication for every managed device, with posture read from Intune, rolled out over roughly 90 to 180 days, monitor mode first. One caution: as of October 21, 2026, several well-known cloud RADIUS offerings have no FedRAMP listing, so confirm before designing around one. The sponsor and CIO choose the platform and decide when NPS retires. The trigger is the Entra migration, not a date, and the replacement must be in place first. The CISO sets the posture requirement. Next, who owns all of this.

title: One decider per row: the network decision register
say: The book's sharpest observation is that the most expensive network mistakes aren't engineering errors. They're ownership gaps: a circuit bought before anyone owned the governor, a cutover before anyone filed the boundary change, a telemetry contract cancelled before anyone confirmed its replacement. Naming one decider for each step is cheaper than any product. The register separates deciding from doing. Network engineering does most of the work, but decides only physics and phasing. The sponsor and CIO decide the governor platforms and the order of branch waves, because those fix cost and the boundary for years. The CISO sets the security envelope every order carries. Security architecture decides the refresh attributes and where each control sits. The authorizing official accepts risk, so four rows land there, including the boundary change, decided before the first production cutover, and the interim gap. Two rows split on purpose. The authorizing official decides whether the boundary may change, but the system owner decides, site by site, whether that site's control layer is live and logging. And telemetry splits between the CISO, security operations and the contracting officer. When a refusal arrives with no control basis, record it as a governance failure, with the refusing role named. Next, how to proceed.

title: Governor before traffic, boundary before cutover
say: How to proceed comes down to order. Order decides whether branch modernization is a gain or a regression. First, secure the governor. The SD-WAN controller is internet-facing with estate-wide authority, so it comes under vulnerability management, privileged access and off-box logging before it carries traffic. Then buy the pipe on measured physics. Deploy the governor before production traffic: a site whose control layer isn't live and logging doesn't get its new egress. Treat the boundary change as the significant change it is, decided before the first cutover. And confirm CISA telemetry parity before any legacy circuit ends. The book is candid that no memo or directive sets this sequence. It's an engineering dependency, and saying so is what makes it survive review. Lighting up fast circuits before the security layer is live is, in the program's experience, the most common and most costly mistake. When funding becomes possible, prove the case in your own estate. Instrument two comparable branches for 30 days, change one, and measure 30 more. That's an effect size a budget examiner will accept. The decision: adopt this order as program policy before the first production cutover. Finally, what can start now.

title: Start now: the work that needs no award
say: Let me close with what can start now, because most of it needs no award. The staff work: write the application-to-path routing policy the controls already ask for. Its absence is the finding, not the absence of a device. Instrument a sample of branches before the next migration wave, and verify that DNS really ends at CISA. Before money moves: send the target attributes, in writing, to whoever scopes the BOD 26-02 replacements, and ask the field-office request to separate acquisition from five-year cost. Before cutover: start CLAW coordination with CISA and the provider, have the authorizing official record the interim gap as an accepted risk, and name one decider per row. One point on urgency. The branch measurement baseline can't be reconstructed after the next migration wave, and it costs staff time, not capital. So, the seven decisions: MTIPS ends on confirmed parity, the interim gap becomes an accepted risk, the refresh carries the target, investment starts with staff time, the field-office request gets tested, NPS retirement follows the Entra migration, and the sequence becomes policy. Buy transport on physics and govern it as compliance, and the branch gets faster without getting weaker. Book 09 has the detail, every claim footnoted, and the backup slides list the sources. Thank you.
